triage.name: Gastroschisis
triage.reason: Newborn with bowel protruding through an abdominal wall defect lateral to the umbilicus; obvious on exam and a surgical emergency, though less of a diagnostic puzzle.

review_issues: presentation: term 'Abnormal prenatal ultrasound' not found in SNOMED CT
presentation: term 'Exposed bowel' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Exposed bowel' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Umbilical cord insertion' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Occurs in about 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 4,000 live births
More common in infants born to young mothers, especially under age 20
Increasing in incidence in recent decades
More common in white and Hispanic infants than in Black infants in US data

risk_factors.text: Maternal use of vasoactive or recreational drugs (e.g., cocaine, amphetamines)
Maternal genitourinary infection during early pregnancy

family_history: Usually none; gastroschisis is generally sporadic and not inherited
exposures: Maternal use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in early pregnancy

chief_complaints.text: My baby was born with the intestines outside the belly
The ultrasound showed the baby's bowel outside the abdomen

hpi.onset: Present at birth; often detected on routine prenatal ultrasound in the second or third trimester
hpi.progression: Stable defect at birth; the exposed bowel is at risk for dehydration, hypothermia, infection, and bowel injury until surgical closure
hpi.location: Abdominal wall, typically to the right of the umbilical cord insertion
hpi.quality: Full-thickness abdominal wall defect with loops of bowel floating freely without a covering sac
relieving: Covering the bowel with a sterile moist dressing

associated_symptoms.text: Bowel loops visible outside the abdomen without a sac

pertinent_negatives: Covering membrane or sac over the bowel (as in omphalocele)
Defect at the umbilicus with cord inserting into the sac
Other major structural anomalies (cardiac, renal, neural tube)

negatives: Umbilical cord inserting into the defect

argues_against: Neonatal sepsis as the primary cause
Congenital heart disease as a primary cause

atypical.how_it_differs: Most cases are diagnosed prenatally; if not, the defect is obvious at birth. Some infants have associated intestinal atresia or malrotation that complicates the appearance.
missing_classic_features: Isolated simple gastroschisis without bowel injury

atypical.how_it_differs: Prenatal ultrasound may show bowel loops floating freely in amniotic fluid, often with polyhydramnios and fetal growth restriction. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein may be elevated.

general.mild: Newborn, alert, vigorous, pink, with bowel visible outside the abdomen; otherwise stable
general.moderate: Newborn with exposed bowel, mildly irritable or lethargic, cool extremities, dry mucous membranes
general.severe: Ill-appearing newborn, lethargic, mottled, with thick matted bowel and signs of dehydration
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale or mottled, hypotensive, with marked hypothermia and shock

findings.maneuver: Inspect the abdomen and umbilical region
findings.finding: Full-thickness abdominal wall defect lateral to the umbilicus, typically to the right of the cord insertion

findings.maneuver: Inspect the defect and its contents
findings.finding: Loops of bowel protruding through the defect without a covering sac or membrane

findings.maneuver: Inspect the herniated viscera for a covering membrane
findings.finding: No sac or membrane covering the bowel (unlike omphalocele)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the umbilical cord insertion relative to the defect
findings.finding: Umbilical cord inserts separately from the defect, not into a sac

findings.maneuver: Press the nail bed or sternum and release
Inspect the skin and mucous membranes
Observe breathing and auscultate the lungs
Examine the scrotum in a male infant

labs.caveat: Leukocytosis is common from stress and inflammation of exposed bowel; a normal count does not exclude sepsis.
Thrombocytopenia may reflect sepsis or disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Low bicarbonate reflects metabolic acidosis from dehydration, hypoperfusion, or bowel ischemia.
Hyponatremia from third-spacing and fluid shifts.
Hypokalemia from vomiting and nasogastric losses; may be hyperkalemic if renal failure or severe acidosis.
Elevated from dehydration and prerenal azotemia.
Neonatal creatinine reflects maternal values early; a rise suggests renal hypoperfusion or injury.
Hypoglycemia is common in stressed, growth-restricted, and premature newborns.
Elevated lactate suggests hypoperfusion, sepsis, or bowel ischemia and should prompt resuscitation.
Supports infection or inflammation but is nonspecific in the first day of life.
Prolonged in sepsis or disseminated intravascular coagulation; check before surgery.
Low fibrinogen with prolonged clotting times suggests disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Arterial or capillary blood gas; acidosis reflects hypoperfusion or bowel ischemia.
Low albumin reflects protein loss and third-spacing in a stressed newborn.

imaging.study: Prenatal ultrasound (obstetric, second or third trimester)
imaging.preferred_when: Routine prenatal screening; usually the first study to detect the defect

findings.text: Loops of bowel floating freely in the amniotic fluid outside the abdominal wall, without a covering membrane
Defect in the abdominal wall lateral to the umbilical cord insertion, usually to the right
Normal umbilical cord insertion separate from the defect
Thickened, dilated, or matted bowel loops suggesting bowel injury
No membrane or sac covering the herniated bowel (distinguishes from omphalocele)

imaging.study: Abdominal x-ray (plain film, supine and lateral decubitus)
imaging.preferred_when: After birth to assess bowel gas pattern and screen for obstruction or perforation

findings.text: Bowel loops visible outside the abdominal wall
Dilated bowel loops suggesting obstruction or ileus
Paucity of bowel gas in the abdomen

imaging.preferred_when: Concern for bowel ischemia, perforation, or intra-abdominal fluid collection
Before surgery if a cardiac anomaly or hemodynamic instability is suspected

findings.text: Normal cardiac anatomy (gastroschisis is usually isolated)

imaging.study: Upper gastrointestinal series or contrast study
imaging.preferred_when: Postoperative or later evaluation of feeding intolerance, obstruction, or malrotation

findings.text: Malrotation with abnormal duodenal-jejunal junction position
Narrowed or obstructed bowel segment (stricture or atresia)

initial.why: Baseline white count, platelets, and hematocrit before surgery; screens for infection and anemia
Assesses dehydration, electrolytes, glucose, and renal function in a newborn with exposed bowel
Screens for hypoperfusion, sepsis, or bowel ischemia
Detects hypoglycemia, common in stressed and growth-restricted newborns

initial.test: Abdominal x-ray (plain film, supine and lateral decubitus)
initial.why: Assesses bowel gas pattern and screens for obstruction or perforation
Evaluates bowel wall, peristalsis, and free fluid
initial.only_if: bowel ischemia, perforation, or intra-abdominal fluid is suspected

confirmatory.test: Prenatal ultrasound (obstetric, second or third trimester)
confirmatory.why: Detects the abdominal wall defect and distinguishes gastroschisis from omphalocele before birth

confirmatory.test: Physical examination of the newborn abdomen
confirmatory.why: Direct visualization of bowel protruding through a defect lateral to the umbilicus without a covering sac confirms the diagnosis at birth

supporting.why: Supports concern for infection or inflammation; trend may guide antibiotics
Assesses acid-base status and oxygenation in an unstable infant
supporting.only_if: respiratory distress or severe metabolic acidosis is present

supporting.why: Screens for structural heart disease before surgery
supporting.only_if: a cardiac anomaly or hemodynamic instability is suspected

not_indicated.why: Radiation and contrast are unnecessary; the diagnosis is clinical and ultrasound/x-ray suffice
Not needed for diagnosis and impractical in an unstable newborn
No role in a congenital abdominal wall defect
Not indicated unless pancreatic injury or obstruction is suspected
Routine urinalysis does not change management in gastroschisis

decision_points: Cover exposed bowel with a sterile moist dressing and place the infant in a plastic wrap or bag to prevent heat and fluid loss
Establish IV access, begin fluid resuscitation, and correct glucose and electrolyte abnormalities before surgery
Give broad-spectrum antibiotics if sepsis or bowel ischemia is suspected
Distinguish gastroschisis from omphalocele: gastroschisis has no covering sac and the cord inserts separately; omphalocele has a sac and the cord inserts into it
Urgent surgical consultation for primary closure or staged silo reduction
Screen for associated anomalies (cardiac, renal, intestinal atresia, malrotation) as clinically indicated

differential.name: Omphalocele
differential.why_considered: Both are congenital abdominal wall defects with exteriorized viscera at birth.
differential.trigger: Any newborn with bowel or organs outside the abdomen — the presence or absence of a covering sac decides the diagnosis.

history: Prenatal ultrasound may show a midline defect at the umbilicus
Associated chromosomal abnormalities (trisomy 13, 18, 21) or other anomalies are common
Maternal diabetes is a risk factor
exam: Herniated viscera covered by a translucent sac or membrane
Umbilical cord inserts into the sac, not separately
Defect is at the umbilicus and may contain liver as well as bowel
Other major anomalies (cardiac, neural tube, renal) may be present
labs: Karyotype or chromosomal microarray may be abnormal
Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein may be elevated
imaging: Prenatal ultrasound shows a membrane-covered midline mass with cord inserting into the sac
Echocardiogram may reveal structural heart disease

differential.name: Umbilical cord hernia
differential.why_considered: A small midline umbilical mass containing bowel can look like a minor abdominal wall defect.

history: Small mass noted at the umbilical cord base at birth
No prenatal detection of a large wall defect
exam: Small sac covered by peritoneum and amnion at the cord base
Contents are usually limited to a small loop of bowel
Cord inserts into the sac
imaging: Ultrasound shows a small midline sac without a lateral full-thickness defect

differential.name: Ruptured omphalocele
differential.why_considered: A ruptured sac leaves uncovered bowel outside the abdomen, mimicking gastroschisis.
differential.trigger: Uncovered bowel with a midline umbilical location and remnants of a sac.

history: Prenatal imaging may have shown a membrane-covered midline mass
Associated anomalies or chromosomal abnormalities may be known
exam: Defect is at the umbilicus, not lateral to it
Torn remnants of a sac or membrane may be visible
Liver may be part of the exteriorized contents
imaging: Prenatal ultrasound documents a midline sac before rupture
Echocardiogram may show structural heart disease

differential.name: Cloacal exstrophy
differential.why_considered: A major lower abdominal wall defect with exteriorized viscera can resemble gastroschisis.
differential.trigger: Exteriorized bowel together with bladder or genital abnormalities.

history: Prenatal ultrasound may show a large lower abdominal wall defect with cystic pelvic structures
Often part of the OEIS complex
exam: Exstrophied bladder halves with exposed mucosa
Ambiguous or abnormal genitalia
Imperforate anus
Defect is lower and more extensive than gastroschisis
labs: Electrolyte and renal function abnormalities from exposed urinary mucosa
imaging: Ultrasound and MRI show bladder exstrophy, spinal defects, and lower abdominal wall defect

differential.name: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
differential.why_considered: Neonatal respiratory distress with bowel outside its normal position can be confused with an abdominal wall defect.
differential.trigger: Severe respiratory distress at birth with bowel in the chest.

history: Prenatal ultrasound may show bowel in the thorax and mediastinal shift
exam: Scaphoid abdomen
Decreased breath sounds on the affected side
Heart sounds displaced
No abdominal wall defect
labs: Respiratory acidosis and hypoxemia on blood gas
imaging: Chest x-ray shows bowel loops in the hemithorax with mediastinal shift
Prenatal ultrasound shows intrathoracic stomach or bowel

differential.name: Prune belly syndrome
differential.why_considered: A lax, thin abdominal wall in a newborn can raise concern for an abdominal wall defect.

history: Prenatal ultrasound may show hydronephrosis and a distended bladder
exam: Wrinkled, lax abdominal wall musculature without a defect
Bilateral undescended testes
Palpable enlarged bladder or kidneys
labs: Elevated creatinine or electrolyte abnormalities from urinary tract obstruction
imaging: Ultrasound shows hydronephrosis, dilated ureters, and a large bladder

differential.name: Physiologic umbilical hernia
differential.why_considered: A protruding umbilical mass in an infant can be mistaken for a wall defect.

history: Appears after the umbilical cord falls off
Intermittent bulge that increases with crying
exam: Skin-covered bulge at the umbilicus
Reducible
No exposed bowel or mucosa
imaging: Ultrasound, if obtained, shows a fascial defect with intact skin

severity.mild: Simple gastroschisis: stable newborn, small defect, bowel minimally thickened, no acidosis, no associated anomalies; primary closure feasible.
severity.moderate: Newborn with moderate bowel edema and matting, mild dehydration or electrolyte abnormality, but no shock or ischemia; staged silo reduction may be needed.
severity.severe: Marked bowel thickening and matting, significant dehydration or metabolic acidosis, suspected bowel ischemia or atresia, or associated anomalies; requires staged repair and intensive support.
severity.critical: Shock, sepsis, severe hypothermia, bowel necrosis or perforation, or multisystem organ failure; immediate resuscitation and emergency surgery.

red_flags.finding: Exposed bowel without a covering sac
red_flags.meaning: Gastroschisis until proven otherwise; requires immediate sterile moist dressing, plastic wrap, and surgical consultation.
Heat loss from exposed viscera; warm the infant and use a plastic wrap or bag.

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or tachycardia with poor perfusion
red_flags.meaning: Shock from dehydration, sepsis, or bowel ischemia; begin fluid resuscitation and antibiotics.
Hypoperfusion or bowel ischemia; urgent surgical evaluation.
Bowel injury or necrosis; may require resection and staged repair.

red_flags.finding: Umbilical cord inserting into a sac
red_flags.meaning: Omphalocele, not gastroschisis; changes workup for associated anomalies and chromosomal testing.

special_populations.differences: Gastroschisis is a disease of newborns; management focuses on thermoregulation, fluid resuscitation, and urgent surgical closure. Preterm birth and growth restriction are common.

Prenatal diagnosis by ultrasound allows delivery planning at a center with pediatric surgery. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein may be elevated. Polyhydramnios and fetal growth restriction may complicate pregnancy.

key_questions.question: Was the defect seen on prenatal ultrasound, and what did it show?
key_questions.looking_for: Bowel loops floating freely outside the abdominal wall without a covering membrane; defect lateral to the cord insertion

key_questions.question: Is the bowel covered by a sac or membrane, or is it exposed?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposed bowel with no covering sac (gastroschisis); a sac suggests omphalocele

key_questions.question: Where is the defect relative to the umbilical cord insertion?
key_questions.looking_for: Defect lateral to the umbilicus, usually to the right, with the cord inserting separately

key_questions.question: When did the defect first appear or get noticed?
key_questions.looking_for: Present at birth; often detected on second- or third-trimester ultrasound

key_questions.question: How was the baby's temperature and hydration at birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypothermia, dry mucous membranes, or poor perfusion from heat and fluid loss

key_questions.question: Has the baby passed meconium or had any bowel movement?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent meconium suggests obstruction, atresia, or bowel injury

key_questions.question: Any vomiting, feeding intolerance, or abdominal distension?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilious vomiting or distension suggesting atresia, malrotation, or obstruction

key_questions.question: Any fever, lethargy, or signs of infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever or hypothermia with lethargy suggesting sepsis

key_questions.question: Were any other anomalies seen on prenatal imaging?
key_questions.looking_for: Cardiac, renal, neural tube, or intestinal anomalies; gastroschisis is usually isolated

key_questions.question: Did the mother smoke, use recreational drugs, or take any medications during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal smoking, cocaine or amphetamine use, or SSRI use as risk factors

key_questions.question: How old is the mother, and was this her first pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Young maternal age, especially under 20, is a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of abdominal wall defects or congenital anomalies?
key_questions.looking_for: Usually none; gastroschisis is generally sporadic

reasoning_points: Newborn with bowel protruding through a full-thickness abdominal wall defect lateral to the umbilicus
No covering sac or membrane over the herniated viscera, distinguishing it from omphalocele
Umbilical cord inserts separately from the defect rather than into a sac
Often detected prenatally on ultrasound as free-floating bowel loops in amniotic fluid
Associated with young maternal age, maternal smoking, and vasoactive drug use
Usually an isolated defect without chromosomal abnormalities or major cardiac, renal, or neural tube anomalies
Requires immediate sterile moist dressing, thermoregulation, fluid resuscitation, and urgent surgical consultation
Complications include dehydration, hypothermia, sepsis, bowel ischemia, intestinal atresia, and malrotation

easy: Newborn with bowel loops visible outside the abdomen without a covering sac
Defect lateral to the umbilicus with cord inserting separately
Prenatal ultrasound showing free-floating bowel in amniotic fluid
Young mother with a history of smoking during pregnancy
medium: Prenatal diagnosis with fetal growth restriction and polyhydramnios
Thickened, matted bowel suggesting bowel injury or atresia
Mild dehydration or electrolyte abnormality at birth
Need to distinguish from omphalocele when the sac is not clearly seen
hard: Ruptured omphalocele mimicking gastroschisis with uncovered bowel
Cloacal exstrophy with exteriorized bowel and bladder or genital abnormalities
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia presenting with respiratory distress and bowel in the chest
Prune belly syndrome with a lax abdominal wall but no true defect
Small umbilical cord hernia mistaken for a minor abdominal wall defect
